docs.title: MIMIQ TensorKeeper
docs.text:
A Clifford-augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) quantum circuit simulator for MIMIQ.

part of MIMIQ, by

TensorKeeper simulates quantum circuits by splitting the state in two:

\[ |\psi\rangle = C \, |\varphi\rangle \]

\(C\) is a Clifford unitary kept as a stabilizer tableau, and \(|\varphi\rangle\) is a Matrix Product State. Clifford gates go into \(C\) at \(O(n)\) and cost no bond dimension, so the MPS only ever has to represent the non-Clifford content of the circuit.

That is the whole point. A Clifford circuit is classically easy by Gottesman-Knill, yet it can be maximally entangled, so a plain MPS simulator pays exponentially for it. TensorKeeper pays nothing. What it pays for instead is magic: \(T\) gates and other non-Clifford operations. On a circuit that is mostly Clifford with bounded magic, it stays cheap at any width and any depth.

It plugs into MIMIQ: you build circuits with mimiqcircuits, run them with TkSimulator, and receive the same QCSResults object MIMIQ uses elsewhere.

New to this? Read Concepts first. It is short, and every tuning knob in the simulator follows from it.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX
from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator

# Build a Bell-state circuit.
c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

sim = TkSimulator(bonddim=64)
results = sim.execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=1)
print(results.histogram())          # {bs"00": ~500, bs"11": ~500}

Both gates are Clifford, so the frame absorbed the entire circuit and the MPS never moved:

state = sim.build_state(2)
state, fidelity = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))
print(state.bond_dim)               # 1
print(fidelity)                     # ExactFidelity()

A Bell pair is entangled, and the residual MPS is still a product state, because all of that entanglement is stabilizer entanglement and lives in the frame.

Add a \(T\) gate and the MPS finally has something to hold, because \(T\) is not Clifford:

from mimiqcircuits import BitString, GateT

c.push(GateT(), 1)
state = sim.build_state(2)
state, _ = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))
print(abs(state.amplitude(BitString("00"))) ** 2)   # 0.5

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• CAMPS core written in Rust, exposed through PyO3. Shared with the Julia binding, so the two agree to machine precision.
  • A conformant mimiqcircuits.backends.LocalBackend: drop-in with the rest of MIMIQ.
  • Clifford gates, Pauli noise, mid-circuit measurement, reset, feed-forward.
  • Expectation values of Pauli strings and of general one- and two-qubit operators, evaluated through the frame without collapsing the state.
  • Amplitudes, bitstring probabilities and sampling.
  • Accuracy reporting that distinguishes an exact run from a truncated one, and never claims exactness it cannot back.

From a source checkout:

cd tensorkeeper-python
uv run maturin develop

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
TensorKeeper is not a better MPS simulator in general. Reach for it when the circuit's difficulty is concentrated:

Workload Use TensorKeeper? Clifford, any depth Yes. Free. Clifford + bounded \(T\) count Yes. This is the design point. Magic state cultivation, error correction Yes. Rotation-dense, magic everywhere No advantage; use TensorWeaver. Small and exact Use a state-vector simulator.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
The public surface is small: one simulator and its GPU variant, one state, and the methods on them. Everything else comes from mimiqcircuits. For how to use these rather than what they are, start with Getting Started.

TkSimulator is a mimiqcircuits.backends.LocalBackend. The interface's abstract members are name, version, capabilities, build_state, compile and evolve; execute is inherited from LocalBackend and built on the last three. compile is pure: no RNG and no sampling, so one compiled circuit serves every shot and every trajectory of a run.

Bitstring ordering

BitString("01") sets qubit 0 to 0 and qubit 1 to 1. The leftmost character is qubit 0. This is the MIMIQ convention, and it is the reverse of Qiskit's.

Bond dimension

TkState.bond_dim and the BondDim instruction report the bond dimension of the residual MPS, not of the physical state. A maximally entangled stabilizer state reads back as 1, because its entanglement is in the Clifford frame. See Concepts.

docs.title: tensorkeeper.TkSimulator
docs.text:
Bases: LocalBackend

Clifford-augmented MPS quantum circuit simulator.

The state is held as |psi> = C |phi>: a Clifford frame C tracked as a stabilizer tableau, and a matrix product state |phi>, the residual, carrying only the nonstabilizerness entanglement. Clifford gates and Pauli noise are absorbed by the frame at O(n) and cost no bond dimension, so a circuit that is mostly Clifford stays cheap however deep and however wide it is. Non-Clifford gates go to the MPS as dressed gates, and they are what you pay for.

The cost model. Bond dimension in |phi> grows with the magic in the circuit, the number and placement of non-Clifford gates, and not with the circuit's depth or with the entanglement of |psi>. That makes this the right simulator for Clifford-dominated workloads (Clifford+T, magic state cultivation, error correction) and the wrong one for circuits whose difficulty is spread everywhere, where it does an ordinary MPS simulator's work and pays a little extra to carry the frame.

Two consequences to absorb before reading any number this backend reports:

  • :attr:.TkState.bond_dim and the BondDim instruction describe |phi>, not |psi>. A maximally entangled stabilizer state reads back as 1. It is the number that governs cost; it is not an entanglement measure.
  • The first few non-Clifford gates on a wide register are usually free. Optimization-free disentangling applies a rotation as a single-qubit gate whenever it can find a qubit where |phi> is still a product state, so bond dimension typically stays at 1 until roughly the register's worth of magic has accumulated, and only then starts to climb.

Usage. There are two entry points, and they do different things:

  • :meth:execute is the MIMIQ driver, inherited from :class:~mimiqcircuits.backends.LocalBackend. It runs the pass pipeline, decides between sampling and trajectory mode, evolves, samples, and hands back :class:~mimiqcircuits.QCSResults. This is what you want almost always.
  • :meth:build_state / :meth:compile / :meth:evolve are the three primitives execute is built from. Drive them yourself when you want one evolution and then many non-destructive queries against the resulting :class:.TkState.

Qubit and classical-bit indices are 0-based, as in mimiqcircuits.

Configuration is construction-only: build a new simulator to change a knob rather than overriding it per call, which keeps the execute keyword surface free of sentinel-versus-explicit collisions.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bonddim int

Maximum bond dimension for the residual MPS, and the value advertised as limits().max_bond_dim. This is the accuracy knob: once the residual would need more than bonddim, compression starts discarding weight and the reported fidelity drops below 1. The default of 256 is comfortable for most Clifford-dominated circuits. It caps |phi>, so a circuit with little magic never approaches it whatever |psi> looks like. Raise it when the fidelity comes back low; lower it to trade accuracy for speed and memory on a deliberately approximate run. Must be positive: limits() has to advertise a positive integer, so a non-positive cap is refused at construction rather than surfacing later as an invalid advertisement.

256 sv_cutoff Optional[float]

Singular values below this fraction of the largest one are discarded during compression, regardless of bonddim. Defaults to :data:DEFAULT_SV_CUTOFF (1e-8), small enough to be numerical hygiene rather than approximation. Raise it (1e-4, 1e-3) to trade a controlled amount of fidelity for a smaller bond dimension on a circuit that is too big at the cutoff you have. It is the gentler of the two truncation knobs, because it drops weight that is genuinely small instead of whatever does not fit. Leave it alone for exact work.

None disentangle_period int | str

How often to run the Clifford disentangler, measured in MPS-touching operations. The disentangler looks for a two-qubit Clifford at each cut that lowers the entropy there, applies it to the MPS and compensates it in the frame. That is an exact re-split of C against |phi>, and it recovers bond dimension which earlier operations left in the residual as gauge rather than magic.

A positive integer N sweeps every N operations; the default, 1, sweeps after each one. "auto" adapts: it sweeps after an operation that grew the bond dimension, the period doubles whenever a sweep fails to reduce it, and resets as soon as one succeeds. 0 disables it.

Keeping the bond dimension low makes every later MPS operation cheaper, since their cost grows as its cube, so the sweeps usually pay for themselves: on msc_d5_noisy a shot is 7x faster with 1 than with 0. Turn it off only for a circuit that never accumulates gauge entanglement. Since it is exact, it can never change the answer on a run that was not truncating.

1 max_num_threads Optional[int]

The most threads a run of this simulator uses, for the linear algebra and for sampling alike. None (default) leaves both to the process setting (the MIMIQ_* thread variables). The cap is held for the length of each :meth:execute and :meth:evolve call and released after, so it never outlives the run. The thread counts are process-wide: simulators running at the same time on different Python threads share them, and each runs at the smallest cap any of them holds.

None linalg Optional[str]

The linear algebra library the residual MPS runs on: "openblas", "mkl" or "faer". None (default) takes whichever engine this installation ships, preferring OpenBLAS, which the wheel bundles. The Windows wheel has no OpenBLAS engine, so there the default is MKL. "mkl" is Intel MKL, whose runtime comes from the mkl package the wheel depends on. "faer" is a pure-Rust library with no system dependency, usually the slowest of the three. Results agree across engines to rounding. A named engine the installation lacks raises :class:ImportError at the first state, rather than switching engine. The resolved name is readable as sim.linalg; :func:tensorkeeper.available_engines lists what is installed.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If bonddim is not positive, max_num_threads is below 1, or linalg is not an engine name.

RuntimeError

On the public kernel-free build, where only :class:~tensorkeeper.MockTensorKeeper runs.

Examples:

A deep, wide Clifford circuit produces a highly entangled state and
costs nothing:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator(bonddim=128)
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> for _ in range(50):
...     for q in range(40):
...         _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), q)
...     for q in range(39):
...         _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)
>>> state, fidelity = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(40), sim.compile(c))
>>> len(c), state.bond_dim
(3950, 1)
>>> type(fidelity).__name__
'ExactFidelity'

The same circuit on a plain MPS simulator would need a bond dimension of
up to ``2**20`` to stay exact.

Driving it through ``execute`` instead, with measurements and shots:

>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.Measure(), 0, 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.Measure(), 1, 1)
>>> results = TkSimulator().execute(c, nsamples=100, seed=42)
>>> sorted(bs.to01() for bs in results.histogram())
['00', '11']
>>> sum(results.histogram().values())
100

docs.title: capabilities()
docs.text:
Capabilities this backend can actually execute.

The MIMIQ driver uses this to decide what to admit, so every token here is a promise that the corresponding operation runs. See :data:TARGET_CAPABILITIES for the intended final set and for why the two are kept as separate literals.

Returns:

Type Description set[str]

A fresh mutable set of capability tokens, all drawn from

set[str]

data:~mimiqcircuits.backends.CAPABILITY_VOCABULARY. It is a copy,

set[str]

so a caller cannot mutate the module state through it.

Examples:

>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> caps = TkSimulator().capabilities()
>>> sorted(caps)[:4]
['amplitude', 'bond_dim', 'classical_bits', 'expectation_1q']

docs.text:
Qubit connectivity: all-to-all.

The MPS is a chain, so a distant pair is reached by a SWAP network rather than being forbidden. Declaring a :class:~mimiqcircuits.backends.LinearChain instead would make callers insert those SWAPs by hand for no gain, since the simulator has to build one anyway.

Returns:

Name Type Description An Topology

>>> from mimiqcircuits.backends import AllToAll
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> isinstance(TkSimulator().topology(), AllToAll)
True

docs.title: can_handle(circuit)
docs.text:
Decline up front what evolve would refuse mid-circuit.

The default check reads the capability set, which is too coarse in two places. Declaring noise admits any Kraus channel, while a Clifford frame can only absorb the mixed-unitary (Pauli) ones: amplitude damping is not a Pauli mixture, so there is nothing to sample into the frame. And a handful of operations belong to no capability token at all, so nothing gates them.

Both would otherwise surface as an opaque failure part-way through a long circuit rather than an admission error before any work is done. Anything this accepts is then subject to the inherited capability check.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default circuit Circuit

The circuit to admit or decline. Only inspected, never modified, and only the first offending operation is reported.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description An AdmissionResult

class:~mimiqcircuits.backends.Admissible verdict, or an

AdmissionResult

class:~mimiqcircuits.backends.Inadmissible one carrying a

AdmissionResult

reason that names the offending operation.

Examples:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from mimiqcircuits.backends import Inadmissible, is_admissible
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> ok = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = ok.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = ok.push(mc.Depolarizing1(0.1), 0)
>>> is_admissible(sim.can_handle(ok))
True

Amplitude damping is a Kraus channel but not a Pauli mixture, so it
is declined before any work is done:

>>> bad = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = bad.push(mc.AmplitudeDamping(0.1), 0)
>>> verdict = sim.can_handle(bad)
>>> isinstance(verdict, Inadmissible)
True
>>> "mixed-unitary" in verdict.reason
True

docs.title: compile(circuit)
docs.text:
Compile a circuit into a form :meth:evolve can run.

Pure, as the interface requires: no RNG, no sampling, no state, and no dependence on anything but circuit. All the real work is per-instruction dispatch that depends on the current Clifford frame, and the frame does not exist until evolution starts (a dressed gate's support is a function of everything before it), so the artifact is mostly a wrapper. It expands containers (GateCall, Block, BlockCall) into the instructions they hold, so a Clifford inside one still goes to the frame. What it adds is a table of the parts that depend on an operation alone (a noise channel's branches, a gate's matrix), filled on first use. The purity is what lets one compiled artifact, and so one table, serve every trajectory (see :meth:recompile_per_trajectory).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default circuit Circuit

The circuit to compile. Not copied and not mutated.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description A CompiledCircuit

class:~mimiqcircuits.backends.CompiledCircuit whose source

CompiledCircuit

is the circuit with its containers expanded.

Examples:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> compiled = TkSimulator().compile(c)
>>> len(list(compiled.source))
1

docs.title: evolve(state, compiled, *, rng=None, callback=None, stopped=None)
docs.text:
Evolve state in place under compiled.

The main loop. Each instruction is routed by _apply_instruction to the classical register, the Clifford frame, or the MPS.

The second return value is the accuracy claim for the run, and its type carries information the number does not:

  • :class:~mimiqcircuits.backends.ExactFidelity: the bonddim cap never bound. Before each operation that can grow a bond, the bonds had room to grow by that operation's full factor. Weight dropped below sv_cutoff does not count against it: that is the requested tolerance. A pure Clifford circuit always reports this.
  • :class:~mimiqcircuits.backends.TruncationLowerBound: the cap bound at least once, and the fidelity is at least the reported value, the weight that survived.

TruncationLowerBound(1.0) is deliberately not ExactFidelity. The claim is about what could have been cut, not about what happened to be: an operation that reached the cap weakens the claim even if it discarded nothing.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state TkState

A :class:.TkState, mutated in place and also returned. It is not reset first, so evolving twice composes the two circuits.

required compiled CompiledCircuit

The artifact from :meth:compile.

required rng Optional[Random]

A :class:random.Random that decides measurements, resets and noise. The call advances it by one draw, which reseeds the core, so two calls sharing one generator draw independent numbers and two generators built from the same seed give the same run. None (default) continues the core's own stream, which starts from operating-system entropy, so the run is not reproducible.

None callback Optional[Callable[..., object]]

Invoked once per instruction as callback(i, total) with a 1-based i, the contract progress.execution_progress_callback documents. Swallowing it leaves progress=True bars frozen.

None stopped Optional[object]

An object with a value attribute; evolution breaks out of the loop as soon as it turns truthy. Used for cooperative cancellation from another thread. A run stopped this way still returns the fidelity accumulated so far.

None

Returns:

Type Description TkState

The (state, fidelity) pair: the same state object that was

Fidelity

passed in, and the accuracy claim described above.

Raises:

Type Description NotImplementedError

If an instruction is one this backend cannot execute, such as a Kraus channel that is not a Pauli mixture. :meth:can_handle rejects the known cases up front, which is the cheaper place to find out.

ValueError

If an IfStatement carries fewer classical bits than its condition needs, or if the core refuses an argument (a malformed gate matrix or Pauli string).

IndexError

If an instruction addresses a qubit outside state.

Examples:

A Clifford circuit is exact, because the MPS is never touched:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
>>> state, fidelity = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(2), sim.compile(c))
>>> type(fidelity).__name__
'ExactFidelity'

Counting the instructions through the callback:

>>> seen = []
>>> _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(2), sim.compile(c),
...                callback=lambda i, total: seen.append((i, total)))
>>> seen
[(1, 2), (2, 2)]

docs.title: expectation(state, op, *qubits)
docs.text:
Return <psi|op|psi> on state, without changing it.

Exact: nothing is sampled, and the value is that of the state as evolved, truncation included. op is conjugated through the Clifford frame rather than applied to the state, so a :class:~mimiqcircuits.PauliString costs one MPS inner product however many qubits it spans, and any other operator on m qubits costs 4**m.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state TkState

A :class:.TkState built by this simulator.

required op

A :class:~mimiqcircuits.PauliString, or any operator with a matrix, such as a gate.

required *qubits int

The 0-based qubits op acts on, in its own leg order, one per qubit of op.

()

Returns:

Type Description complex

The complex expectation value.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the number of qubits does not match op.

Examples:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(2), sim.compile(c))
>>> sim.expectation(state, mc.PauliString("XX"), 0, 1)
(1+0j)
>>> abs(sim.expectation(state, mc.GateZ(), 0))
0.0

docs.title: simplify_pass()
docs.text:
The pass execute(simplify=True) installs.

The default pass also resynthesizes gate runs into GateU and GateCX. A GateU is not recognized as a Clifford even at Clifford angles, so it would move gates the frame absorbs for free onto the MPS. This keeps only the passes that never change gate types: removing identities, cancelling inverse pairs and merging rotations, which turns T T into S and so moves gates into the frame.

Returns:

Name Type Description A

class:~mimiqcircuits.SimplifyPass.

Examples:

Two ``T`` gates merge into an ``S``, which the frame absorbs:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from mimiqcircuits.backends.passes import PassContext
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateT(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateT(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> simplified, _ = TkSimulator().simplify_pass().apply(PassContext(), c)
>>> [type(i.operation).__name__ for i in simplified]
['GateS', 'GateH']

docs.title: recompile_per_trajectory(circuit)
docs.text:
Whether each trajectory needs its own compile.

Always False. Mixed-unitary noise is resolved by sampling a Pauli into the Clifford frame at runtime, inside :meth:evolve, rather than by baking a chosen branch into the compiled artifact, so one compile serves every shot and the driver can hoist it out of the trajectory loop.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default circuit Circuit

The circuit about to be run. Ignored; the answer does not depend on its contents.

required

Returns:

Type Description bool

False.

Examples:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.Depolarizing1(0.1), 0)
>>> TkSimulator().recompile_per_trajectory(c)
False

docs.title: GPU simulator
docs.text: TkSimulatorGpu is TkSimulator with the residual MPS on an NVIDIA GPU: same arguments, same capabilities, same results. Check gpu_available first.

docs.title: tensorkeeper.TkSimulatorGpu
docs.text:
Bases: TkSimulator

Clifford-augmented MPS simulator with the residual MPS on an NVIDIA GPU.

The same simulator as :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulator, with the same arguments, capabilities and results. Every state it builds keeps its residual MPS |phi> in device memory for the whole run: through evolution, sampling, and the resets between shots. The Clifford frame stays on the host, since a frame update is a few word operations per qubit and never reads the MPS.

When it pays. The device does the MPS work, so it helps when that work is large: a circuit with enough magic to push the bond dimension up. On a Clifford-dominated circuit whose residual stays small, the CPU simulator is as fast or faster, because there is little MPS work to move.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bonddim int

As for :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulator.

256 sv_cutoff Optional[float]

As for :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulator.

None disentangle_period int | str

As for :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulator.

1 max_num_threads Optional[int]

As for :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulator.

None linalg Optional[str]

The host library under the device engine. The CUDA engine is built on OpenBLAS, so this must be None (default) or "openblas"; sim.linalg reads "openblas".

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If bonddim is not positive, or linalg names a library other than OpenBLAS.

RuntimeError

If :func:tensorkeeper.gpu_available is False: this installation has no CUDA engine, or no device is reachable through it. The message says which, and what to install. Refused here rather than falling back to the CPU, so a run never reports GPU timings that were CPU ones.

Examples:

Pick the GPU when there is one:

>>> import tensorkeeper as tk
>>> sim = tk.TkSimulatorGpu() if tk.gpu_available() else tk.TkSimulator()
>>> sim.name in ("TensorKeeper", "TensorKeeperGpu")
True

docs.title: tensorkeeper.gpu_available()
docs.text:
Whether this process could use a GPU.

True means this installation carries the CUDA engine and a device is reachable through it now. Every way of not having one (a CPU-only wheel, no driver, no CUDA libraries, no card) reports False, so this is safe to call anywhere and never raises. The first call probes for a device, which takes a moment when there is a CUDA engine to probe with.

:class:TkSimulatorGpu requires this to be True.

Type Description bool

True if a GPU is usable by the core, False otherwise.

>>> import tensorkeeper as tk
>>> isinstance(tk.gpu_available(), bool)
True

docs.title: tensorkeeper.TkState
docs.text:
Bases: State

A CAMPS state plus the classical and complex registers.

The quantum register is the Clifford frame and MPS pair held in the Rust core, reached through :attr:core. The classical bits are a :class:~mimiqcircuits.BitString and the z-variables a list of complex numbers, both of which the MIMIQ driver writes into directly and then copies into results.cstates / results.zstates.

You rarely construct one of these. :meth:.TkSimulator.build_state does it for you, and execute does that in turn. Building one by hand is worth it when you want to evolve a circuit and then interrogate the resulting state repeatedly: :meth:amplitude, :meth:probability and the expectation values are all non-destructive, so a single evolution can answer many questions.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default num_qubits int

Size of the quantum register. A zero-qubit state is legal but useless, so the core is always built with at least one site.

required num_bits int

Size of the classical bit register. Every bit starts at 0.

0 num_zvars int

Size of the complex z-register. Every entry starts at 0j.

0 bonddim int

Maximum bond dimension for the residual MPS |phi>.

256 sv_cutoff float

Singular values below this fraction of the largest one are discarded during compression.

1e-08 disentangle_period int | str

Clifford-disentangler schedule; see :class:.TkSimulator for what the three forms mean.

1 usegpu bool

Move the residual MPS to the GPU at construction, and again after every :meth:reset. :class:.TkSimulatorGpu sets it.

False engine ModuleType | None

The native module to build the core from. Defaults to the one usegpu selects: the CUDA engine if set, the default CPU engine otherwise.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If disentangle_period is neither a non-negative integer nor "auto".

Attributes:

Name Type Description core CampsCore

The Rust CAMPS state, from the engine's module. Everything below delegates to it; reach for it directly only when you need a primitive this class does not wrap.

Examples:

Build a two-qubit state, evolve a Bell pair onto it, and read the
result back three different ways:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
>>> state = sim.build_state(2)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))
>>> round(state.probability(mc.BitString("00")), 6)
0.5
>>> round(state.expectation_paulistring("ZZ", [0, 1]).real, 6)
1.0
>>> state.bond_dim
1

The last line is what the simulator buys: a Bell pair is entangled, but
it is a *stabilizer* state, so all of its entanglement sits in the
Clifford frame and the residual MPS is still a product state at
``chi = 1``.

docs.title: core property
docs.text:
The underlying Rust CAMPS state.

The escape hatch for primitives this class does not wrap: the per-bond profile from core.bond_dims(), the raw Clifford application in core.apply_clifford(code, qubits), and so on. Nothing on it is part of the stable Python API; prefer the methods on this class where they exist.

docs.title: num_qubits property
docs.text: Number of qubits in the quantum register.

docs.title: num_bits property
docs.text: Number of classical bits.

docs.title: num_zvars property
docs.text: Number of complex z-variables.

docs.title: classical_bits property
docs.text:
The classical bit register, as a live mutable bitstring.

Measurements write here, the classical-logic operations (Not, Xor, …) read and write here, and IfStatement conditions are evaluated against it. The driver copies this object into results.cstates once per trajectory.

docs.title: complex_values property
docs.text:
The complex z-register, as a live mutable list.

ExpectationValue, Amplitude and BondDim write their results here; Add, Multiply and Pow do arithmetic on it. The driver copies it into results.zstates.

docs.title: bond_dim property
docs.text:
The largest MPS bond dimension currently in use.

This is a property of the residual |phi>, not of the physical state |psi>. Entanglement carried by the Clifford frame is invisible to it, so a maximally entangled stabilizer state reads back as 1. That is the useful number, since it is what the simulator actually stores and what :meth:.TkSimulator.limits caps, but it is not the state's Schmidt rank, and it must not be reported as an entanglement measure.

Typically far below the cap: only nonstabilizerness reaches the MPS, so a Clifford-dominated circuit stays near 1 however deep it runs.

Returns:

Type Description int

The largest bond dimension over all cuts of |phi>, at least

int

1. For the full per-cut profile, use core.bond_dims().

Examples:

A GHZ state on eight qubits is entangled across every cut, and a
plain MPS would need ``chi = 2``. Here the whole circuit is
Clifford, so the residual never leaves ``chi = 1``:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> for q in range(7):
...     _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(8), sim.compile(c))
>>> state.bond_dim
1

docs.title: is_on_device property
docs.text:
Whether the residual MPS currently lives in GPU memory.

False for a partly moved state, so this answers "can this be operated on without transfers", not "is any of it on the device".

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if every site tensor is device-resident.

docs.title: to_device()
docs.text:
Move the residual MPS onto the GPU for the rest of the run.

The Clifford frame stays on the host. It is a bit-packed tableau updated in O(n) word operations, so there is nothing for a GPU to do with it, and a Clifford gate never reads the MPS, so that path costs no transfer at all.

Worth doing only if the state then stays there for a stretch of circuit: a round trip costs more than the work it would feed. Move once, evolve, read at the end. Reads are what to watch, since :meth:prob_bitstring and sampling walk the register on a copy.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

if this build has no GPU backend, if no device is reachable, or if the upload fails. Call :func:tensorkeeper.gpu_available to tell the first two apart from a transient failure.

docs.title: to_host()
docs.text:
Bring the residual MPS back to host memory.

Succeeds on a state that is already on the host, and in a build with no GPU backend, where there is nothing to bring back.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

if the download fails.

docs.title: amplitude(bs)
docs.text:
Amplitude <bs|psi> of a computational-basis state.

The read-out itself is exact, whatever truncation the evolution may have done. Its cost is exponential in the stabilizer entanglement of the Clifford frame rather than in the qubit count, which is the price of a computational-basis amplitude for this representation: the frame is what turns one basis state of |psi> into a superposition over |phi>.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bs BitString

A :class:~mimiqcircuits.BitString, or any iterable of 0/1 of length :attr:num_qubits. Bit q is qubit q, 0-based.

required

Returns:

Type Description complex

The complex amplitude <bs|psi>.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If bs is not exactly :attr:num_qubits long.

Examples:

``T H |0>`` puts a phase of ``exp(i pi/4)`` on the ``|1>`` branch:

>>> import math
>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateT(), 0)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(1), sim.compile(c))
>>> a0 = state.amplitude(mc.BitString("0"))
>>> a1 = state.amplitude(mc.BitString("1"))
>>> round(abs(a0), 6) == round(abs(a1), 6) == round(1 / math.sqrt(2), 6)
True
>>> round(math.degrees(math.atan2(a1.imag, a1.real)))
45

Computed directly rather than by squaring :meth:amplitude, so it is the right call when the phase is not wanted.

required

The probability, in [0, 1].

Raises:

If bs is not exactly :attr:num_qubits long.

Examples:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(2), sim.compile(c))
>>> [round(state.probability(mc.BitString(b)), 6)
...  for b in ("00", "01", "10", "11")]
[0.5, 0.0, 0.0, 0.5]

docs.title: expectation_paulistring(spec, qubits)
docs.text:
<psi|P|psi> for a Pauli string P over qubits.

The cheap observable. P is conjugated through the Clifford frame, which maps it to another Pauli string, so the whole thing costs one MPS inner product no matter how wide P is and no matter how scrambled the frame. The state is not disturbed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spec str

Pauli letters, one per entry of qubits, from "IXYZ". Case-insensitive. Letter k applies to qubits[k].

required qubits Sequence[int]

The qubit indices spec applies to, 0-based. Need not be contiguous or sorted.

required

Returns:

Type Description complex

The expectation value. Real up to rounding for a Hermitian P,

complex

but returned as a complex number so a phase error is visible rather

complex

than silently discarded.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If spec and qubits differ in length, or spec holds a letter that is not a Pauli symbol.

IndexError

If a qubit index is outside the register.

Examples:

A Bell pair is a ``+1`` eigenstate of both ``ZZ`` and ``XX``, while
either qubit alone is unpolarized:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(2), sim.compile(c))
>>> round(state.expectation_paulistring("ZZ", [0, 1]).real, 6)
1.0
>>> round(state.expectation_paulistring("XX", [0, 1]).real, 6)
1.0
>>> abs(state.expectation_paulistring("Z", [0])) < 1e-12
True

docs.title: expectation_operator(matrix, qubits)
docs.text:
<psi|O|psi> for an arbitrary 1- or 2-qubit operator O.

O is decomposed into Paulis and summed, so it never has to be expanded over its dressed support. The price is 4**len(qubits) inner products rather than one. Prefer :meth:expectation_paulistring when the operator already is a Pauli string. The state is not disturbed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default matrix Sequence[Sequence[complex]]

The operator, flattened column-major over qubits, with the first entry of qubits the most significant leg. So 4 values for one qubit and 16 for two.

required qubits Sequence[int]

One or two qubit indices, 0-based.

required

Returns:

Type Description complex

The expectation value. Complex for the same reason as in

complex

meth:expectation_paulistring: a non-Hermitian O, or a phase

complex

error, stays visible.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If matrix does not hold 4**len(qubits) entries.

IndexError

If a qubit index is outside the register.

Examples:

The projector onto ``|00>`` has expectation ``0.5`` on a Bell pair,
and it is a genuine mixture of Pauli terms rather than a single
string:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(2), sim.compile(c))
>>> p00 = [0j] * 16
>>> p00[0] = 1 + 0j
>>> round(state.expectation_operator(p00, [0, 1]).real, 6)
0.5

A single-qubit ``Z`` agrees with its Pauli-string form, which is the
useful cross-check when a hand-written matrix is suspect:

>>> z = [1 + 0j, 0j, 0j, -1 + 0j]
>>> matrix_form = state.expectation_operator(z, [0])
>>> pauli_form = state.expectation_paulistring("Z", [0])
>>> abs(matrix_form - pauli_form) < 1e-12
True

docs.title: sample(nsamples, rng=None)
docs.text:
Sample nsamples computational-basis bitstrings.

The state is not disturbed: each draw collapses a throwaway copy, so repeated calls are independent samples of the same state and every read-out method still works afterwards. This is what makes execute cheap on a purely unitary circuit, which evolves once and then samples.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default nsamples int

How many bitstrings to draw. 0 returns an empty list.

required rng Optional[Random]

A :class:random.Random to draw from. The call advances it by one draw, which reseeds the core, so two calls sharing one generator give different samples and two generators built from the same seed give the same ones. None (default) continues the core's own stream, which starts from operating-system entropy.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description list[BitString]

A list of nsamples :class:~mimiqcircuits.BitString objects,

each list[BitString]

attr:num_qubits long, with bit q holding qubit q.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If nsamples is not an integer.

ValueError

If nsamples is negative.

Examples:

A GHZ state only ever yields all-zeros or all-ones, and two
generators with the same seed yield the same draws:

>>> import random
>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> for q in range(3):
...     _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(4), sim.compile(c))
>>> draws = state.sample(200, random.Random(1234))
>>> sorted({b.to01() for b in draws})
['0000', '1111']
>>> state.sample(5, random.Random(7)) == state.sample(5, random.Random(7))
True

docs.title: reset()
docs.text:
Reset every register to its zero value, reusing the allocation.

This is what the driver calls between shots. The quantum register is rebuilt in the core rather than reset qubit by qubit: the latter leaves the Clifford frame in place and the accumulated fidelity untouched, which across shots would charge later shots for an earlier shot's truncation.

The configuration and the RNG stream survive, so consecutive shots stay distinct.

Examples:

>>> import mimiqcircuits as mc
>>> from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
>>> sim = TkSimulator()
>>> c = mc.Circuit()
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
>>> _ = c.push(mc.GateT(), 1)
>>> state, _ = sim.evolve(sim.build_state(2), sim.compile(c))
>>> state.reset()
>>> round(state.probability(mc.BitString("00")), 6)
1.0

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Every capability below is declared and executes. Anything absent is refused, by can_handle where it can be detected before the run starts.

Capability Instruction it enables amplitude Amplitude sampling sampling from the final state classical_bits Not, And, Or, Xor, SetBit0, SetBit1, ReadoutErr zvars Add, Multiply, Pow midcircuit_measure Measure, MeasureX, MeasureY, MeasureXX, MeasureYY, MeasureZZ, MeasurePauli midcircuit_reset Reset, ResetX, ResetY, PrepareStateT reset_after_measure MeasureReset, MeasureResetX, MeasureResetY feed_forward IfStatement noise mixed-unitary (Pauli) Kraus channels only bond_dim BondDim expectation_1q ExpectationValue of a 1-qubit operator expectation_2q ExpectationValue of a 2-qubit operator expectation_paulistring ExpectationValue of a PauliString

Not supported, and declined by can_handle: SchmidtRank, VonNeumannEntropy, WhileStatement, and any non-mixed-unitary Kraus channel.

The capability set TensorKeeper is being built towards.

A MIMIQ capability is a promise: declaring one commits the backend to executing every operation that belongs to it. This literal records the intended final set so it can be read as a roadmap, and so a conformance test can check the whole set against :data:~mimiqcircuits.backends.CAPABILITY_VOCABULARY rather than only the part that works today.

Every entry is also implemented today, so what :meth:TkSimulator.capabilities returns is equal to this, but the two stay separate literals on purpose. The comment above the assignment says why an over-declaration is the dangerous direction.

docs.title: Fidelity
docs.text:
evolve returns (state, fidelity), where the fidelity is one of mimiqcircuits.backends' two types:

Type Meaning ExactFidelity() the bonddim cap never bound; weight below sv_cutoff is the requested tolerance TruncationLowerBound(v) the cap bound at least once; the fidelity is at least v

Once the cap has bound, the claim is TruncationLowerBound and never ExactFidelity, and TruncationLowerBound(1.0) is deliberately not ExactFidelity(). See Accuracy and Tuning.

docs.title: tensorkeeper.thread_info(linalg=None)
docs.text:
How each thread pool resolved, and what decided it.

The engine runs two pools. core is the linear algebra: gate application, compression, decompositions. sampler draws shots from the evolved state. Each entry carries source, what decided the count, and threads, the count itself or None where the library sized itself. core also carries effective, the count the linear algebra actually runs on.

Each pool takes, in order, its own MIMIQ_CORE_NUM_THREADS or MIMIQ_SAMPLER_NUM_THREADS, then MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS, then the native variable of the library underneath, then the library's own default. source is "limit" while a simulator's max_num_threads holds the count below that. docs.title: tensorkeeper.qiskit.TensorKeeperBackend(*, gpu=False, mock=False, name='tensorkeeper', num_qubits=64, seed=None, **tk_options)
docs.text:
Build a Qiskit BackendV2 backed by a TensorKeeper simulator.

The returned backend converts each QuantumCircuit to a MIMIQ circuit and runs it on :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulator. Wrap it in Qiskit's BackendSamplerV2 for sampling, or use :class:~tensorkeeper.qiskit.TensorKeeperEstimator for expectation values.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default gpu bool

Run on :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulatorGpu, with the residual MPS on an NVIDIA GPU. Raises at construction when no GPU is usable. Default False.

False mock bool

Run on :class:~tensorkeeper.MockTensorKeeper instead. It takes the same options and refuses the same inputs, needs no licence, and simulates nothing: every result is the all-zero outcome. For tests of the plumbing around a backend; see the "Without a licence" page of the manual. Default False; it cannot be combined with gpu.

False name str

Backend name reported to Qiskit.

'tensorkeeper' num_qubits int

Qubit count advertised on the Qiskit Target.

64 seed int | None

Default for the seed run option, readable as backend.options.seed. Every run forwards it to the simulator's execute, so two runs of the same circuits give the same results; run(qc, seed=...) overrides it for one call. None (default) draws fresh entropy per run.

None **tk_options

Options of the simulator, fixed at construction: bonddim, sv_cutoff, disentangle_period, max_num_threads and linalg, as :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulator describes them. An option it does not take raises :class:TypeError.

{}

Returns:

Type Description 'MimiqBackend'

A configured mimiq_qiskit.MimiqBackend.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If both gpu and mock are set.

Example::

from qiskit.primitives import BackendSamplerV2

backend = TensorKeeperBackend(bonddim=64, seed=1)
counts = backend.run(qc, shots=1000).result().get_counts()

# Same options, no licence, no simulation: for CI.
ci = TensorKeeperBackend(mock=True, bonddim=64)

docs.title: tensorkeeper.qiskit.TensorKeeperEstimator
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEstimatorV2

Qiskit EstimatorV2 backed by the TensorKeeper CAMPS simulator.

On a circuit that ends in a definite state, results are exact up to the MPS truncation set by tk_options: no term is sampled, whatever its weight, so the reported standard errors are zero and the only error left is the truncation, reported as min_fidelity in the result metadata.

A circuit carrying a mid-circuit measurement, a reset or a noise channel ends in an ensemble, and its expectation value is the average over the trajectories TensorKeeper evolves, one per shot. That average is the unbiased estimate of :math:\mathrm{Tr}(\rho O), so it is what this reports, with the sample standard error in stds. Reading one trajectory would be unbiased too but as noisy as the observable's own range, so a stochastic circuit with no budget raises rather than returning it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default simulator

An existing TensorKeeper simulator to use as is, in which case tk_options must be empty and gpu and mock false. None (default) builds one from them.

None gpu bool

Evaluate on :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulatorGpu, with the residual MPS on an NVIDIA GPU. Default False.

False mock bool

Evaluate on :class:~tensorkeeper.MockTensorKeeper instead. It takes the same options and refuses the same inputs, needs no licence, and simulates nothing: every expectation value is 0. For tests of the plumbing around a backend; see the "Without a licence" page of the manual. Default False.

False method str

"auto" (default) evaluates exactly when the circuit is deterministic and averages trajectories when it is not. "exact", "trajectories" and "shots" force one of the three, as documented in :mod:mimiq_qiskit.estimation.

'auto' trajectories int | None

Trajectories to average for a stochastic circuit. None sizes it from precision. Ignored for a deterministic circuit, which has one answer however many times it is run.

None shots int | None

Shots per measurement basis, estimating from measurements in rotated Pauli bases the way hardware and Qiskit's BackendEstimatorV2 do. Giving this selects that method. For a given budget it is noisier than averaging trajectories, since it samples the observable as well as the ensemble; it is the right choice for reproducing a shot-based reference.

None emulate_shot_noise bool

Add Gaussian noise of width precision to an otherwise exact value, as Qiskit's StatevectorEstimator does. One evolution rather than a shot budget, for code that wants to see plausible shot noise without paying for it.

False default_precision float

Precision used when run is called without one. A positive value sizes the trajectory or shot budget as ceil(1/precision**2), Qiskit's convention. The default, 0.0, asks for the exact value.

0.0 seed int | None

Seed forwarded to every run, and to the emulate_shot_noise generator. Expectation values consume no randomness, so it only matters for a circuit that carries noise or mid-circuit measurements. None (default) draws fresh entropy.

None **tk_options

Options of the simulator, fixed at construction: bonddim, sv_cutoff, disentangle_period, max_num_threads and linalg, as :class:~tensorkeeper.TkSimulator describes them. An option it does not take raises :class:TypeError.

{}

Result metadata reports method, whether the value is exact, whether the run was stochastic, the trajectories or shots spent, the target_precision, and min_fidelity: the lowest MPS fidelity behind the pub. That last one is the truncation error, which averaging more trajectories does not reduce; raise bonddim for that.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Read this page before the rest of the manual. Every tuning knob and every performance surprise in TensorKeeper follows from what is here.

It assumes you are comfortable with quantum circuits and have a rough picture of a Matrix Product State: a chain of tensors whose bond dimension \(\chi\) grows with entanglement. If MPS is new, read TensorWeaver's concepts page first. TensorKeeper uses TensorWeaver for the MPS half of its state.

docs.title: The problem with entanglement as a cost model
docs.text:
An MPS pays for entanglement. Bond dimension \(\chi\) across a cut must be at least the Schmidt rank there, so a state that is highly entangled across every cut is expensive no matter how simple it was to prepare.

That cost model is a good one for most circuits. It is a bad one for Clifford circuits.

A Clifford circuit is built from \(H\), \(S\) and \(\text{CNOT}\) (and anything they generate: \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\), \(\text{CZ}\), \(\text{SWAP}\), and so on). By the Gottesman-Knill theorem, such a circuit is classically simulable in polynomial time. It is easy. Yet a Clifford circuit can produce a state that is maximally entangled across every cut, needing \(\chi = 2^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}\) in an MPS.

So a plain MPS simulator can be defeated by a circuit that is provably easy. It spends exponential memory storing entanglement that carries no hard information.

docs.title: The CAMPS factorization
docs.text:
TensorKeeper splits the state in two:

\[ |\psi\rangle = C \, |\varphi\rangle \]
  • \(C\) is a Clifford unitary, stored as a stabilizer tableau. It costs \(O(n^2)\) bits, and applying a Clifford gate to it costs \(O(n)\). Entanglement in \(C\) is free.
  • \(|\varphi\rangle\) is an MPS, called the residual. It carries only what \(C\) cannot.

This is the Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State of Liu & Clark, Classical simulability of Clifford+T circuits with Clifford-augmented matrix product states, Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023116 (2026).

A pure Clifford circuit now costs nothing: every gate goes into \(C\), and \(|\varphi\rangle\) stays \(|0\dots0\rangle\) at \(\chi = 1\), however deep the circuit runs. The exponential blow-up is gone because the representation finally matches what the theorem says about the difficulty.

docs.title: Magic is the resource
docs.text:
If Clifford gates are free, what is not?

Non-Clifford gates. \(T\), controlled-phase at a generic angle, Toffoli. The quantity that governs cost is nonstabilizerness, also called magic: how far the state is from being a stabilizer state. In TensorKeeper this is concrete. Bond dimension in \(|\varphi\rangle\) grows with the magic in the circuit, not with its entanglement and not with its depth.

That gives a sharp design point. A circuit that is mostly Clifford with a bounded amount of magic stays cheap at any width and any depth:

Circuit Plain MPS TensorKeeper Clifford, any depth up to \(\chi = 2^{n/2}\) \(\chi = 1\) Clifford + a few \(T\) large \(\chi\) \(\chi\) set by the \(T\) count Magic everywhere large \(\chi\) large \(\chi\), plus frame overhead

The last row is the honest one. TensorKeeper is not a better MPS simulator in general. On a circuit whose difficulty is genuinely spread everywhere it does the same work as an MPS and pays a little extra to carry the frame. Use it where the magic is sparse: Clifford+\(T\), magic state cultivation, error correction.

Magic also does not have to be paid for the moment it arrives. On a wide register the first non-Clifford gates are typically absorbed at no bond cost at all, so \(\chi\) can sit at 1 for a while and only then start to climb. \(\chi = 1\) therefore does not mean "no magic": a product residual can carry plenty of it. How long the free run lasts depends on the circuit, and it is of order \(n\) rather than exactly \(n\).

docs.title: Where each operation goes
docs.text:
Every operation is routed to whichever half can absorb it cheaply.

Operation Goes to Cost Clifford gate the frame, \(C \leftarrow GC\) \(O(n)\), MPS untouched Pauli noise the frame, after sampling one branch \(O(n)\), MPS untouched Non-Clifford gate \(G\) the MPS, as the dressed gate \(\hat G\) depends on \(\hat G\)'s support Measurement, reset both: a Pauli read from the frame, a projector on the MPS

The interesting case is the third.

docs.title: Dressed gates
docs.text:
A non-Clifford gate \(G\) acts on \(|\psi\rangle\), but the MPS holds \(|\varphi\rangle\). Pushing \(G\) through the frame gives

\[ G \, |\psi\rangle = G C |\varphi\rangle = C \, (C^\dagger G C) \, |\varphi\rangle = C \, \hat G \, |\varphi\rangle , \]

so the MPS sees the dressed gate \(\hat G = C^\dagger G C\) and the frame is unchanged.

Conjugation by a Clifford maps Paulis to Paulis, so \(\hat G\) stays easy to describe. It need not act on the same qubits as \(G\), though. A \(T\) gate on one qubit can dress into an operator whose support spans much of the register, because the frame has scrambled that qubit's \(X\) and \(Z\) images across the chain.

That is the one asymmetry to keep in mind: support width is not gate width. TensorKeeper never expands \(\hat G\) into a dense \(2^k\) matrix over its support. Its cost is exponential in the width of the original gate (1 for \(T\), 2 for controlled-phase, 3 for Toffoli) and only linear in the width of the dressed support. Wide dressed support costs time, not memory.

docs.title: Disentangling: why bond dimension does not have to grow
docs.text:
Two mechanisms keep \(|\varphi\rangle\) small. Both are exact: they change the split between \(C\) and \(|\varphi\rangle\), never \(|\psi\rangle\).

Optimization-free disentangling (OFD) applies when a rotation \((\alpha I + \beta P)\) lands on the MPS. Whenever the residual is still a product state somewhere in \(P\)'s support, the rotation goes on as a single-qubit gate with no bond growth at all, and the rest of \(P\) is absorbed by the frame. A \(T\) gate on a fresh qubit is therefore free, not merely cheap. This is what makes the early \(T\) gates on a wide register cost nothing.

The Clifford disentangler (OBD) runs as a periodic sweep. At each cut it looks for a two-qubit Clifford that lowers the entropy there, applies it to the MPS and compensates it in the frame. This recovers entanglement that earlier operations left in \(|\varphi\rangle\) but that is really gauge, not magic. It is on by default, after every operation on the MPS; see Accuracy and Tuning.

docs.title: What bond dimension means here
docs.text:
state.bond_dim reports the bond dimension of \(|\varphi\rangle\), not of \(|\psi\rangle\).

This is the number that matters for cost, and it is the one limits().max_bond_dim caps. It is not the physical state's Schmidt rank. A maximally entangled stabilizer state reads back as \(\chi = 1\), because all of its entanglement lives in the frame. So do not read a physical entanglement measure off the bond dimension. This backend declines SchmidtRank and VonNeumannEntropy outright, rather than answer them about \(|\varphi\rangle\) when the question is about \(|\psi\rangle\).

The same caveat applies to the BondDim circuit instruction.

docs.title: Truncation and fidelity
docs.text:
Two settings bound the MPS: a maximum bond dimension bonddim, and a singular-value cutoff sv_cutoff. When a compression discards weight, the result is approximate, and evolve says so in its second return value:

  • ExactFidelity(): the bonddim cap never bound, so nothing it would cut was ever at risk. A pure Clifford circuit always reports this.
  • TruncationLowerBound(v): the cap bound at least once, and the fidelity is at least v.

Weight below sv_cutoff is the tolerance you set and counts against neither. TruncationLowerBound(1.0) is deliberately not ExactFidelity(). The claim is about what could have been cut, not what happened to be. The two settings, what the bound is worth, and how to confirm a run has converged are covered in Accuracy and Tuning.

docs.title: Relationship to MIMIQ and TensorWeaver
docs.text:
TensorKeeper is a MIMIQ backend. It implements mimiqcircuits.backends.LocalBackend, so it takes the same Circuit objects and returns the same QCSResults as any other backend, and you can swap it for one without changing your circuit code.

The MPS half is TensorWeaver, used as a library. The Clifford half is a tableau in TensorKeeper's Rust core. Both bindings, Python and Julia, sit on that one core, so they agree numerically to machine precision.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
Read 01 to 08 if you are new to the simulator. The arc is: build and run (01), understand the cost model (02, 03), then the operations that need more than a unitary (04, 05, 06), then observables (07), then accuracy (08).

If you already know CAMPS and want specific things:

  • 02 and 03 are the pair that shows what makes TensorKeeper different from an MPS simulator. If you read only two, read these.
  • 08 for the accuracy and fidelity contract, before you trust a number.
  • 06 if your workload is noisy: the supported-channel restriction is a real constraint, and better met here than mid-project.

The Julia examples in tensorkeeper-julia/examples/ mirror these one for one. Reading a pair side by side is a good way to learn the simulator across both bindings.

docs.title: Circuit Execution
docs.text: What the simulator accepts, how measurement and noise are handled, and how to read results back.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
execute does three things:

  1. Compile. compile(circuit) wraps the circuit for evolution. It is pure: no randomness, no sampling, no state. The same compiled circuit serves every shot.
  2. Evolve. Each instruction is routed to the Clifford frame, the MPS, or the classical registers, per the table in Concepts.
  3. Read out. Measurement outcomes land in the classical register, observables in the complex register, and both are collected into a QCSResults.

docs.title: Execution modes
docs.text: MIMIQ picks the mode from the circuit's content.

docs.title: Sampling mode
docs.text:
A circuit with no mid-circuit randomness is evolved once, then sampled nsamples times. Trailing measurements are stripped and replaced by sampling the final state, which is much cheaper than repeating the evolution.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX
from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

sim = TkSimulator()
results = sim.execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=1)
print(results.histogram())

docs.title: Trajectory mode
docs.text:
A circuit containing noise, mid-circuit measurement, reset or feed-forward is evolved once per shot, because each shot follows a different branch. This is nsamples times the work of sampling mode.

The state is reused across shots and reset between them, so the frame, the MPS and the accumulated fidelity all start fresh each time.

docs.title: Supported operations
docs.text:
The declared capabilities cover amplitudes and sampling, the classical bit and complex z registers, mid-circuit measurement and reset in the \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) bases, feed-forward through IfStatement, mixed-unitary (Pauli) noise, the BondDim instruction, and expectation values of Pauli strings and of general one- and two-qubit operators. API Reference lists the exact token-to-instruction mapping.

Every declared capability executes, and anything not declared is refused. Where it can be detected up front, the refusal comes from can_handle before any work is done rather than part-way through a long run:

from mimiqcircuits import AmplitudeDamping

c = Circuit()
c.push(AmplitudeDamping(0.1), 0)
print(sim.can_handle(c))
# Inadmissible(reason='backend TensorKeeper supports only mixed-unitary (Pauli)
# noise; AmplitudeDamping cannot be absorbed into a Clifford frame')

docs.title: Measurement and reset
docs.text:
Measurement is the one operation that touches both halves of the state. The measured Pauli is read from the frame, and the corresponding projector is applied to the MPS.

from mimiqcircuits import Measure

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)         # qubit 0 -> classical bit 0
c.push(Measure(), 1, 1)

results = sim.execute(c, nsamples=100, seed=1)
print(results.histogram())       # only bs"00" and bs"11": perfectly correlated

Reset is not local

Reset measures the qubit and then flips it conditionally. If the qubit is entangled with the rest of the register, that measurement projects the rest of the register onto the sampled branch. The reset qubit ends in \(|0\rangle\) deterministically; the other qubits do not. This is physics, not an implementation choice, and it surprises people.

Pauli-product measurements, MeasureXX, MeasureYY, MeasureZZ and MeasurePauli, run as a Clifford basis change, a single-qubit measurement and the inverse basis change. All of it happens in the frame, so a stabilizer measurement costs no bond dimension.

PrepareStateT puts a qubit in the magic state \(T|+\rangle\) whatever its previous state: a reset, then H in the frame, then T on the MPS. The reset leaves the qubit a product state, so the T lands on a free pivot and costs no bond dimension either.

docs.title: Noise
docs.text:
Only mixed-unitary channels are supported: those expressible as a probabilistic mixture of unitaries, which for a Clifford frame means Pauli mixtures. Depolarizing, PauliX, PauliNoise and friends qualify.

Such a channel costs nothing. One Pauli branch is sampled per shot and folded into the frame at \(O(n)\), leaving the MPS untouched. Noise is therefore free in the same sense a Clifford gate is, and a noisy Clifford circuit still runs at \(\chi = 1\).

from mimiqcircuits import Depolarizing1

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(Depolarizing1(0.05), 0)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)

results = sim.execute(c, nsamples=2000, seed=1)
print(results.histogram())

A general Kraus channel such as AmplitudeDamping cannot be written as a Pauli mixture, so there is nothing to sample into the frame. TensorKeeper refuses it rather than approximating it: silently simulating different physics is worse than an error.

docs.title: Observables
docs.text:
ExpectationValue computes \(\langle\psi|O|\psi\rangle\) without collapsing or copying the state. The operator is conjugated through the frame instead of being applied, so a Pauli string costs one MPS inner product.

from mimiqcircuits import ExpectationValue, PauliString

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(ExpectationValue(PauliString("ZZ")), 0, 1, 0)   # -> z-variable 0
c.push(ExpectationValue(PauliString("XX")), 0, 1, 1)

state = sim.build_state(2, 0, 2)
state, _ = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))
print(state.complex_values)      # [1+0j, 1+0j]: both correlators are +1

A general one- or two-qubit operator works too. It is Pauli-decomposed into \(4^m\) terms for \(m\) qubits, each term free in the frame:

from mimiqcircuits import GateZ, GateCZ

c.push(ExpectationValue(GateZ()), 0, 2)
c.push(ExpectationValue(GateCZ()), 0, 1, 3)

The operator must be Hermitian to be an observable at all.

docs.title: Reading the state directly
docs.text:
Outside a circuit, query the state:

import random
from mimiqcircuits import BitString

state = sim.build_state(2)
state, _ = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))

state.amplitude(BitString("00"))                     # complex
state.probability(BitString("00"))                   # float
state.sample(100, random.Random(1))                  # list of BitString
state.expectation_paulistring("ZZ", [0, 1])          # complex
state.expectation_operator([1, 0, 0, -1], [0])       # column-major 1q operator
state.bond_dim                                       # int

sample does not destroy the state: each draw collapses a throwaway copy, so the state stays queryable afterwards.

These read-outs do not all cost the same, and the factorization is why. A Pauli string is conjugated through the frame into another Pauli string, so expectation_paulistring is one MPS inner product however wide the string and however scrambled the frame. A computational-basis amplitude is the expensive one: the frame turns a single basis state of \(|\psi\rangle\) into a superposition over \(|\varphi\rangle\), so its cost is exponential in the stabilizer entanglement of the frame rather than in the qubit count. Both are exact, whatever truncation the evolution did.

docs.title: Randomness
docs.text:
Randomness belongs to the call, not to the simulator: a TkSimulator holds no seed. What a call is given decides what it draws.

Passed Result seed=7 (execute only) The same seed gives the same results, every time. rng=generator The call advances the generator. Two calls sharing one generator differ; two generators built from the same seed agree. neither Fresh entropy. Two calls differ and neither can be repeated.

execute takes seed= or rng=, a random.Random. The calls below it, TkSimulator.evolve and TkState.sample, take rng only.

import random
from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator

sim = TkSimulator()

a = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, seed=7)
b = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, seed=7)      # identical to `a`

# One generator for a whole script: rerunning the script repeats every run,
# and the runs still differ from one another.
rng = random.Random(7)
c = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, rng=rng)
d = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, rng=rng)     # differs from `c`

# A simulation split over several calls continues one stream, so the
# measurements of the second part are independent of those of the first.
rng = random.Random(7)
state = sim.build_state(n, nbits)
state, _ = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(first_part), rng=rng)
state, _ = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(second_part), rng=rng)
shots = state.sample(1000, rng)

Building a new generator from the same seed for each part would hand both parts the same random numbers, and their measurement outcomes would be correlated. Pass the generator along instead.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
execute returns a mimiqcircuits.QCSResults:

Field Contents histogram() measured bitstrings and their counts cstates the classical register, one entry per shot zstates the complex register, one entry per shot fidelities one fidelity per shot amplitudes amplitudes for any bitstrings you requested

The fidelity entries are the accuracy claim for each shot; see Accuracy and Tuning for what the number is worth.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
execute takes the standard MIMIQ driver arguments. The ones that matter here:

Parameter Meaning nsamples shots in sampling mode, trajectories in trajectory mode seed seeds the run: the same seed gives the same results; see Randomness rng a random.Random to draw the run's seed from, advanced by the call; passing both is a TypeError callback called once per instruction as callback(i, total), with a 1-based i progress display a progress bar, driven by that callback simplify cancel inverse pairs, drop identities and merge rotations before the run; see below

simplify=True runs a reduced version of MIMIQ's simplification pass. The default pass also resynthesizes gate runs into GateU, which this backend cannot recognize as Clifford, so it would move frame work onto the MPS. The reduced pass only ever turns gates into the frame's favor: T T becomes S.

execute also takes a SweepExperiment, and returns one result per point of its parameter table.

Accuracy settings are not per-call. bonddim, sv_cutoff and disentangle_period are fixed when the simulator is constructed, so build a new TkSimulator to change one. So is max_num_threads, which caps the threads a run of that simulator uses for the linear algebra and for sampling.

docs.title: Free-threaded Python
docs.text:
CPython 3.14 supports a build with no global interpreter lock. On it Python threads run at the same time on different cores, so one process can run several simulations in parallel without starting a process per run.

TensorKeeper supports it. This page covers installing the right wheel, the one thing you currently have to do to keep the GIL off, and the rule your code has to follow.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Free-threaded interpreters carry a t suffix, python3.14t, and are a separate installation from python3.14 with their own packages.

python3.14t -m pip install mimiq-tensorkeeper --index-url https://mimiq:<your-token>@license.qperfect.io/pypi/simple

There is nothing to select. A dedicated free-threaded wheel is published, and the installer picks it by tag:

Interpreter Wheel python3.11 … python3.14 cp311-abi3, one wheel for every version python3.14t cp314-cp314t, Linux x86_64: glibc 2.35 or newer, and glibc 2.34 for RHEL 9

It exists separately because a free-threaded interpreter has no stable ABI, so the wheel serves exactly one Python version. It carries the same engines as the ordinary Linux wheel: OpenBLAS, MKL, faer and CUDA. The two cannot be mixed up: python3.14t does not accept an abi3 wheel, and reports no matching distribution rather than installing one that would crash.

Free-threaded wheels are built for Linux x86_64 only; ask us if you need macOS or Windows.

docs.title: Keeping the GIL off: PYTHON_GIL=0
docs.text:
A free-threaded interpreter turns the GIL back on, for the whole process, when it imports an extension module that has not declared itself safe without it, and warns when it does:

RuntimeWarning: The global interpreter lock (GIL) has been enabled to load
module 'symengine.lib.symengine_wrapper', which has not declared that it can
run safely without the GIL.

TensorKeeper's engines declare it, so importing tensorkeeper never causes this. symengine does not yet, and mimiqcircuits imports it to build gate matrices, so import mimiqcircuits re-enables the GIL for the life of the process. Until symengine declares support, override that at startup:

PYTHON_GIL=0 python3.14t my_simulation.py
# or
python3.14t -X gil=0 my_simulation.py

and check it took before trusting a timing:

import sys
import mimiqcircuits as mc
import tensorkeeper as tk

print(sys._is_gil_enabled())   # must be False

PYTHON_GIL=0 overrides every module's declaration in the process, which is why it is opt-in. Keep symbolic work out of your threads: build and parametrize circuits before starting them.

docs.title: One simulator per thread
docs.text:
A state must be driven by one thread at a time. States hold no shared data, so threads that each own theirs never interact. Two threads driving the same state is refused rather than silently corrupting it:

RuntimeError: Already borrowed

Give each thread its own simulator, which builds its own state:

import threading
import tensorkeeper as tk

def run(seed, results, index):
    sim = tk.TkSimulator(bonddim=256)
    results[index] = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000, seed=seed)

results = [None] * 8
threads = [threading.Thread(target=run, args=(s, results, i)) for i, s in enumerate(range(8))]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

Sharing the Circuit, as above, is fine: execute only reads it.

docs.title: What threading buys
docs.text:
TensorKeeper holds the GIL for every call into its engine, so on an ordinary python3.14 threads take turns and running eight of them is no faster than running them one after another. On python3.14t with the GIL off they run concurrently.

Each simulation also calls into a multi-threaded BLAS, so n Python threads on c cores can ask for far more threads than there are cores. Cap each simulator with TkSimulator(max_num_threads=c // n), or set MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS for the process. The cap is process-wide: simulators running at the same time share it, and each runs at the smallest one held.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page installs the package and runs a circuit through both API paths. If the terms Clifford frame, dressed gate or magic are new, read Concepts first; this page assumes them.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer.
  • mimiqcircuits, which supplies Circuit, the gate set and QCSResults.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Wheels are published on tagged releases. Install with the token that came with your licence:

pip install mimiq-tensorkeeper --index-url https://mimiq:<your-token>@license.qperfect.io/pypi/simple

The index serves every QPerfect product your licence covers and forwards every other name to PyPI, so dependencies resolve from the same URL. To avoid repeating it:

pip config set global.index-url https://mimiq:<your-token>@license.qperfect.io/pypi/simple

then pip install mimiq-tensorkeeper. With uv, pass the same URL as --index, or set UV_INDEX_URL.

The distribution is mimiq-tensorkeeper; the package you import is tensorkeeper.

Use --index-url, not --extra-index-url. Public PyPI carries the same name as an unlicensed mock (see Without a licence), and with both indexes in play pip may take either copy. tk.has_kernels() is True on the licensed wheel.

Wheels exist for:

Platform Python Engines Linux x86_64, glibc 2.35+ and glibc 2.34 (RHEL 9) 3.11 and later, 3.14t OpenBLAS, MKL, faer, CUDA macOS arm64 (macOS 26 or newer) 3.11 and later OpenBLAS, faer Windows x86_64 3.11 and later MKL, faer

On Linux x86_64 and Windows the wheel depends on Intel's mkl package, which pip installs with it: MKL cannot be bundled into a wheel. For TkSimulatorGpu, install the CUDA libraries too; the NVIDIA driver comes from the system:

pip install "mimiq-tensorkeeper[cuda]" --index-url https://mimiq:<your-token>@license.qperfect.io/pypi/simple

A free-threaded interpreter (python3.14t) gets its own wheel automatically; see Free-threaded Python.

docs.title: Choosing an engine
docs.text:
The residual MPS runs on a linear algebra library, and each library is a separate engine in the wheel. TkSimulator(linalg=...) picks one per simulator:

import tensorkeeper as tk

print(tk.available_engines())       # e.g. ['openblas', 'mkl', 'faer', 'cuda']
sim = tk.TkSimulator(linalg="mkl")  # "openblas", "mkl", "faer", or None
print(sim.linalg)                   # the engine it will run on

linalg=None, the default, takes OpenBLAS where the wheel has it and MKL on Windows. MKL is often faster on Intel CPUs; faer is pure Rust, needs nothing from the system, and is usually the slowest. All three give the same results to rounding. tk.library_info() and tk.compile_info() say what an engine is and how it was built; quote them in a bug report.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
cd tensorkeeper-python
uv run maturin develop
uv run pytest tests/ -q

maturin develop compiles the OpenBLAS engine and installs the package in editable mode. Rebuild it after any change to tensorkeeper-rs. It builds no documentation, so tk.docs_dir() is empty there.

docs.title: Two ways in
docs.text: TensorKeeper offers the same two paths as any MIMIQ backend.

docs.title: High level: execute
docs.text:
execute runs the circuit and returns a QCSResults, handling shots, trajectories and measurement bookkeeping for you. Use it unless you need the state itself.

from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateCX, Measure
from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(Measure(), 0, 0)
c.push(Measure(), 1, 1)

sim = TkSimulator(bonddim=64)
results = sim.execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=1)

print(results.histogram())      # {bs"00": ~500, bs"11": ~500}
print(results.fidelities[0])    # 1.0

docs.title: Lower level: build_state + compile + evolve
docs.text:
These are the three primitives execute is built from. Drive them yourself when you want one evolution followed by many queries against the resulting state. Nothing is sampled and nothing is hidden.

from mimiqcircuits import BitString

c = Circuit()
c.push(GateH(), 0)
c.push(GateCX(), 0, 1)

sim = TkSimulator(bonddim=64)
state = sim.build_state(2)                     # |00>
state, fidelity = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))

print(state.amplitude(BitString("00")))        # (0.7071+0j)
print(state.probability(BitString("11")))      # 0.5
print(state.bond_dim)                          # 1
print(fidelity)                                # ExactFidelity()

amplitude, probability, the expectation values and sample are all non-destructive, so one evolution can answer many questions.

compile is pure: no randomness, no sampling, no state. That is what lets a single compiled circuit serve every shot of a run.

docs.title: Seeing the Clifford frame work
docs.text:
The point of TensorKeeper is visible in one number. Build a deep Clifford circuit and watch the bond dimension stay at 1.

import random
from mimiqcircuits import Circuit, GateH, GateS, GateCX, GateCZ
from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator

rng = random.Random(0)
n = 40
c = Circuit()
for q in range(n):
    c.push(GateH(), q)
for _ in range(400):                            # 400 random Clifford gates
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        q = rng.randrange(n - 1)                # a neighboring pair
        c.push(rng.choice([GateCX(), GateCZ()]), q, q + 1)
    else:
        c.push(rng.choice([GateH(), GateS()]), rng.randrange(n))

sim = TkSimulator()
state = sim.build_state(n)
state, fidelity = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))

print(state.bond_dim)     # 1: the frame absorbed all 440 gates
print(fidelity)           # ExactFidelity()

40 qubits, 440 gates, a state that is highly entangled, and the MPS never left \(\chi = 1\). A plain MPS simulator would need a bond dimension in the thousands for the same circuit.

Now add magic. A handful of \(T\) gates on a register this wide is still free:

from mimiqcircuits import GateT

for q in range(0, n, 8):                        # 5 T gates
    c.push(GateT(), q)

state = sim.build_state(n)
state, fidelity = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))
print(state.bond_dim)     # still 1
print(fidelity)           # ExactFidelity()

Bond dimension climbs only once enough magic has accumulated, which on \(n\) qubits takes of order \(n\) non-Clifford gates:

for q in range(n):                              # a full T layer, 40 more
    c.push(GateT(), q)

state = sim.build_state(n)
state, fidelity = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))
print(state.bond_dim)     # 2: the T gates now cost bond dimension
print(fidelity)           # TruncationLowerBound(value=1.0)

Two lessons in those three runs. Cost tracks magic, not depth and not entanglement. And the fidelity claim weakened to TruncationLowerBound at the first truncating operation even though its value is exactly 1.0 and no accuracy was lost, which is a distinction worth understanding before you rely on the number: see Accuracy and Tuning.

state.bond_dim is the bond dimension of the residual MPS \(|\varphi\rangle\), not of the physical state. See Concepts.

docs.title: Qubit and bit indices
docs.text:
Indices are 0-based in Python, matching mimiqcircuits. c.push(GateH(), 0) acts on the first qubit.

Bitstring ordering

BitString("01") has qubit 0 set to 0 and qubit 1 set to 1. The leftmost character is qubit 0. This is the MIMIQ convention and is the reverse of Qiskit's.

docs.text:
