  • Accuracy and Tuning: when to change bonddim, sv_cutoff or disentangle_period.
  • Examples: runnable scripts in a deliberate order.

docs.title: MockTensorKeeper
docs.text:
MockTensorKeeper is TensorKeeper's interface with nothing behind it. It takes the same constructor and the same execute call as TkSimulator, refuses exactly what TkSimulator refuses, and returns a real QCSResults full of nothing: all-zero samples, zero amplitudes and expectation values, fidelity 1.0.

It is for validating the data models, what a MIMIQ backend accepts and what it hands back, on a machine that has no licence. That is a common shape of acceptance test: a CI job checks that its circuits build, that its options are accepted, and that its results parse and round-trip, with no interest in the physics.

import mimiqcircuits as mc
from tensorkeeper import MockTensorKeeper

sim = MockTensorKeeper(bonddim=64, disentangle_period="auto")

c = mc.Circuit()
c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(mc.Measure(), [0, 1], [0, 1])

res = sim.execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=42)

res.simulator        # 'MockTensorKeeper'
len(res.cstates)     # 1000, every one a real BitString
res.histogram()      # {bs"00": 1000}
res.saveproto("out.pb")

Swapping it for the real thing is a one-line change, because the two take the same arguments:

from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator as Sim       # licensed
from tensorkeeper import MockTensorKeeper as Sim  # unlicensed CI

MockTkSimulator is the same class under the name that matches TkSimulator. examples/00_mock_backend walks through it.

docs.title: What it guarantees
docs.text:
It subclasses TkSimulator and overrides only the places where physics would happen: build_state, which returns a MockState whose read-outs answer zero, and evolve, which leaves the state alone. Everything that defines the interface is inherited, so the two cannot drift apart:

  • the constructor, with all its arguments and checks: a bonddim, linalg or max_num_threads TensorKeeper rejects is rejected here;
  • capabilities(), limits(), topology() and can_handle(), so admission and the anti-capability sweep every MIMIQ backend runs give identical verdicts;
  • execute() and the whole LocalBackend driver, which chooses between the sampling and trajectory routes and builds the QCSResults itself.

tests/test_mock.py asserts those methods are inherited rather than overridden, and that the constructor takes TkSimulator's arguments.

What it does not do is compute. It is not an approximation or a fast mode. Nothing is simulated.

docs.title: The public wheel
docs.text:
MockTensorKeeper is in every build, licensed or not, so one test suite can run against both. It is also the only backend in the wheel published on public PyPI:

pip install mimiq-tensorkeeper

No token, no index URL, no licence. The same wheel is also published as mimiq-tensorkeeper-mock, for projects that need the licensed package and the mock under different names; Testing shows both setups. That wheel is the only one built with --features no-kernels: gate application, the Clifford frame updates, measurement, sampling, noise and expectation values are kept from the compiler by #[cfg], in the CAMPS core and in the MPS core under it, rather than stripped afterwards. What is left is a zero CAMPS state and its read-only accessors. TkSimulator refuses to construct there and says so.

Before it can be published, the release audit (scripts/build_wheel.py --audit-only) loads each engine in the wheel and requires has_kernels() to be False with every compute method of CampsCore absent, and scans every file in the wheel for those method names and for the source paths of the removed modules.

docs.title: Which wheel am I running?
docs.text:
The two distributions share a name and a version number, so pip install mimiq-tensorkeeper works both with and without the QPerfect index configured. They are told apart at runtime:

public PyPI QPerfect index tk.has_kernels() False True TkSimulator() raises RuntimeError works MockTensorKeeper() works works licence required none yes

Install the licensed wheel with an exclusive --index-url, as Getting Started shows, not --extra-index-url: with both indexes in play, pip may take either copy of a name it finds in both.

docs.title: MIMIQ TensorKeeper: unlicensed mock
docs.text:
This distribution on PyPI is not the TensorKeeper simulator. It is MockTensorKeeper: the same interface, the same arguments, the same MIMIQ data models, and no simulation behind them. Results come back well-formed and empty: all-zero samples, zero amplitudes and expectation values, fidelity 1.0.

It exists so that code which drives a MIMIQ backend can be tested on a machine with no licence: a CI job can check that its circuits build, that its options are accepted, and that its results parse and round-trip, without paying for a simulation it does not care about.

pip install mimiq-tensorkeeper

The same build is also published as mimiq-tensorkeeper-mock. Use that name when a project declares the licensed package (mimiq-tensorkeeper, from QPerfect) and this mock side by side and needs the two to have different names. Install one or the other, never both: they install the same tensorkeeper package.

import mimiqcircuits as mc
from tensorkeeper import MockTensorKeeper

sim = MockTensorKeeper(bonddim=64)

c = mc.Circuit()
c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
c.push(mc.Measure(), [0, 1], [0, 1])

res = sim.execute(c, nsamples=1000, seed=42)
res.histogram()        # {bs"00": 1000}: a real QCSResults, carrying nothing

MockTensorKeeper takes the same constructor and execute arguments as the licensed TkSimulator and refuses exactly what it refuses, so a configuration that fails here fails there. Swapping between them is an import change.

docs.title: What this build cannot do
docs.text:
It is compiled without the compute kernels: gate application, the Clifford frame updates, measurement, sampling, noise and expectation values are not in the binary. tensorkeeper.has_kernels() is False, and TkSimulator raises on construction and says so.

python -m tensorkeeper.examples.00_mock_backend.main runs in this build; the other examples in tensorkeeper.examples_dir() show what the licensed one does.

docs.title: The licensed simulator
docs.text:
TensorKeeper is a Clifford-augmented matrix product state quantum circuit simulator for MIMIQ, distributed by QPerfect to licence holders from its own package index rather than from PyPI.

For access, documentation and support: https://qperfect.io

docs.title: Qiskit integration
docs.text:
The optional tensorkeeper.qiskit module runs Qiskit circuits on TensorKeeper. A QuantumCircuit is converted to a MIMIQ circuit and evolved, so your Qiskit code stays unchanged.

Install the extra:

pip install 'mimiq-tensorkeeper[qiskit]'

Bit ordering

Qiskit's own convention applies to Qiskit objects: counts keys come back with the highest-indexed qubit on the left, the reverse of the MIMIQ ordering TensorKeeper uses natively. The conversion handles this, so read Qiskit results as Qiskit results.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
TensorKeeperBackend is a Qiskit BackendV2. Simulator options (bonddim, sv_cutoff, disentangle_period and the rest listed under Choosing a simulator) are fixed when the backend is built. run takes shots, seed and memory, and the circuit-preparation options of TkSimulator.execute, such as simplify.

seed is a run option, not a simulator option. TensorKeeperBackend(seed=1) sets its default, so every run of that backend is seeded with 1 and repeats exactly; backend.run(qc, seed=2) overrides it for one call. Left unset, each run draws fresh entropy.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from tensorkeeper.qiskit import TensorKeeperBackend

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure_all()

backend = TensorKeeperBackend(bonddim=64, seed=1)
counts = backend.run(qc, shots=4000).result().get_counts()

It also works under Qiskit's V2 primitives:

from qiskit.primitives import BackendSamplerV2

sampler = BackendSamplerV2(backend=backend)
result = sampler.run([qc], shots=4000).result()[0]
counts = result.data.meas.get_counts()

docs.title: Expectation values
docs.text:
TensorKeeperEstimator is an EstimatorV2. Every Pauli term is read exactly from the state, whatever its weight, so there is no shot noise and the reported standard errors are zero. The only error is the MPS truncation itself, set by bonddim and sv_cutoff, and reported as min_fidelity in the result metadata.

The terms are cheap as well as exact. A Pauli term is conjugated through the Clifford frame into another Pauli string and read off the MPS with one inner product, so a term on every qubit costs about as much as a term on one, and the frame's entanglement costs nothing at all (see Concepts). That is what makes large observables on Clifford-heavy circuits, such as stabilizer codes with a few non-Clifford gates, practical.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
from tensorkeeper.qiskit import TensorKeeperEstimator

qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.t(1)
qc.ry(0.7, 2)

obs = SparsePauliOp.from_list([("ZZI", 1.0), ("IIZ", 0.5), ("XYZ", 0.25)])

estimator = TensorKeeperEstimator(bonddim=64)
result = estimator.run([(qc, obs)]).result()[0]
print(result.data.evs, result.data.stds)

An estimator pub carries state preparation, not readout, so a measurement left at the end of the circuit is dropped rather than collapsing the state the observable is read from.

docs.title: Circuits that end in an ensemble
docs.text:
That exactness needs the circuit to end in one definite state. A mid-circuit measurement, a reset or a noise channel makes TensorKeeper re-evolve the circuit once per shot, and each trajectory has its own expectation value. The quantity you want, Tr(rho O), is their average, so the estimator needs a budget to estimate it:

Argument What it does trajectories=N Average N trajectories. Each contributes an exact value, so only the ensemble is sampled. stds is the standard error of the mean. shots=N Estimate from measurements in rotated Pauli bases, N shots per basis, as hardware and Qiskit's BackendEstimatorV2 do. Terms that commute qubit-wise share a basis, so an observable needing several costs N shots in each. precision=p Size either budget as ceil(1/p**2), Qiskit's convention. method=... Force "exact", "trajectories" or "shots" instead of letting "auto" choose from the circuit. 
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.h(0)
qc.measure(0, 0)   # state preparation, not readout: the x follows it
qc.x(0)

obs = SparsePauliOp("Z")   # -1 or +1 per trajectory, 0 over the ensemble

averaged = TensorKeeperEstimator(trajectories=4000, seed=1)
result = averaged.run([(qc, obs)]).result()[0]
print(result.data.evs, "+/-", result.data.stds)

sampled = TensorKeeperEstimator(shots=4000, seed=1)   # the same quantity

Given no budget, a stochastic circuit raises rather than returning one trajectory as though it were exact. method="exact" forces that single-trajectory read anyway, with a warning: it is an unbiased draw, but its spread is the observable's own range, not a small error.

For the same budget, averaging trajectories is never worse than sampling and is usually better, because sampling adds the observable's shot noise on top of the ensemble's, and it runs one basis rather than several. Reach for shots= when you need to reproduce what a shot-based estimator would report, not for accuracy.

docs.title: Reading the metadata
docs.text:
{'target_precision': 0.0,
 'method': 'trajectories',   # or 'exact', 'shots'
 'exact': False,             # True only with no statistical error at all
 'stochastic': True,         # one evolution per shot was needed
 'trajectories': 4000,       # or 'shots': N
 'min_fidelity': 0.998}      # lowest MPS fidelity behind the pub

min_fidelity is the truncation error, not a statistical one. Averaging more trajectories does not improve it; raising bonddim does. See Accuracy and Tuning for what drives it.

precision and default_precision do not change an exact value: a deterministic circuit has one answer and no shot budget to spend on it. To see plausible shot noise on such a circuit without paying for it, emulate_shot_noise=True adds Gaussian noise of width precision to the exact value, the way Qiskit's StatevectorEstimator does, for the cost of one evolution.

To reuse a configured simulator across both interfaces, pass it in rather than repeating the options:

from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator
from tensorkeeper.qiskit import TensorKeeperEstimator

sim = TkSimulator(bonddim=128)
estimator = TensorKeeperEstimator(simulator=sim)

The estimator reads each term with TkSimulator.expectation, which you can also call yourself on a state from evolve.

docs.title: Choosing a simulator
docs.text:
Both TensorKeeperBackend and TensorKeeperEstimator take the options of TkSimulator, fixed for the life of the backend or estimator:

Option Default Meaning bonddim 256 Maximum bond dimension of the residual MPS, the memory and accuracy knob. Lowering it truncates earlier and lowers the reported fidelity. sv_cutoff None (1e-8) Singular values below this fraction of the largest are discarded. disentangle_period 1 How often the Clifford disentangler sweeps: every N MPS operations, "auto", or 0 for never. See Accuracy and Tuning. max_num_threads None The most threads a run uses. None leaves it to the process setting. linalg None Linear-algebra library: "openblas", "mkl" or "faer". None takes the preferred one this build ships.

An option TkSimulator does not take raises TypeError. On the estimator, seed is its own argument rather than a simulator option, and simulator may be an existing simulator instance, used as is; no options, gpu or mock may be passed with one.

gpu=True runs on TkSimulatorGpu, with the residual MPS on an NVIDIA GPU. It raises at construction when no GPU is usable rather than falling back to the CPU.

mock=True runs on MockTensorKeeper instead. It takes the same options and refuses the same inputs, needs no licence, and simulates nothing: every shot is the all-zero outcome and every expectation value is 0. It is for testing the code around a backend in CI; see Without a licence. It cannot be combined with gpu.

import os
from tensorkeeper.qiskit import TensorKeeperBackend

mock = os.environ.get("TK_MOCK") == "1"
backend = TensorKeeperBackend(mock=mock, bonddim=64)

docs.title: Gate coverage
docs.text: Conversion covers the standard Qiskit gate set. Custom gates and gates with unbound parameters raise mimiq_qiskit.converter.UnsupportedGateError: bind the parameters and decompose custom gates before running.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
A test suite that drives TensorKeeper usually runs in two places: on a machine with a licence, where circuits are really simulated, and in CI, where there is often no licence and no wish to spend minutes simulating. MockTensorKeeper serves the second case. It takes the same arguments as TkSimulator, refuses the same inputs, and returns real QCSResults without simulating anything; Without a licence describes exactly what it guarantees.

This page covers how to set up a project and its tests around the two.

docs.title: One suite, two backends
docs.text:
Pick the backend in one place, a fixture, and let every test take it. An environment variable makes the choice explicit:

# conftest.py
import os

import pytest
import tensorkeeper as tk

MOCK = os.environ.get("TK_MOCK") == "1"


@pytest.fixture
def simulator():
    # Same keywords for both: a knob the real simulator rejects is rejected
    # by the mock too, so CI catches it without a licence.
    cls = tk.MockTensorKeeper if MOCK else tk.TkSimulator
    return cls(bonddim=64)


# For tests that check physics rather than plumbing.
needs_simulation = pytest.mark.skipif(MOCK, reason="MockTensorKeeper simulates nothing")

# test_pipeline.py
import mimiqcircuits as mc

from conftest import needs_simulation


def bell():
    c = mc.Circuit()
    c.push(mc.GateH(), 0)
    c.push(mc.GateCX(), 0, 1)
    c.push(mc.Measure(), [0, 1], [0, 1])
    return c


def test_results_round_trip(simulator, tmp_path):
    # Plumbing: runs the same against the mock and the real simulator.
    res = simulator.execute(bell(), nsamples=100, seed=1)
    assert len(res.cstates) == 100
    res.saveproto(tmp_path / "out.pb")


@needs_simulation
def test_bell_correlations(simulator):
    # Physics: the mock returns all-zero samples, so this only means
    # something on the real simulator.
    res = simulator.execute(bell(), nsamples=1000, seed=1)
    assert {bs.to01() for bs in res.cstates} == {"00", "11"}

Run TK_MOCK=1 pytest in CI and plain pytest on a licensed machine.

Use an explicit switch like TK_MOCK rather than detecting the licence. tk.has_kernels() says whether the build can simulate, not whether a licence is present: it is True for the licensed package on a machine without a licence, where TkSimulator then refuses at the first run.

docs.title: The same package everywhere
docs.text:
MockTensorKeeper is in every build, so the licensed package serves both sides. Without a licence it imports, the mock runs, and only TkSimulator refuses. Nothing in the project changes between the two environments: install mimiq-tensorkeeper from the QPerfect index as described in Getting Started, and set TK_MOCK=1 in CI.

Without a licence, importing tensorkeeper prints one line to standard error, tk: license init failed: .... It is expected and does not stop the mock.

This is the simplest setup whenever CI can reach the QPerfect index or the wheel file.

docs.title: CI without access to the licensed package
docs.text:
If CI cannot reach the QPerfect index, it can install the public build from PyPI instead. It holds the same tensorkeeper module with every compute kernel left out, so the mock is the only backend that runs on it. It is published under two names with the same contents: mimiq-tensorkeeper, the licensed package's own name, and mimiq-tensorkeeper-mock.

Never install the public and the licensed build in one environment, under either name: they write the same files. Under two different names, nothing warns you about it.

docs.title: Under its own name
docs.text:
mimiq-tensorkeeper-mock lets a project declare both builds without any index configuration. With pip, keep them in separate requirements files, one per environment. In a uv project, two dependency groups that exclude each other do it from one pyproject.toml and one lockfile. Here the licensed build comes as a wheel file:

[dependency-groups]
licensed = ["mimiq-tensorkeeper"]
mock = ["mimiq-tensorkeeper-mock"]

[tool.uv]
# Both install the `tensorkeeper` package, so they can never be installed
# together.
conflicts = [[{ group = "licensed" }, { group = "mock" }]]

[tool.uv.sources]
mimiq-tensorkeeper = { path = "wheels/mimiq_tensorkeeper-<version>-<tags>.whl" }

The wheel file is needed to create or update the lockfile, not to install the mock:

uv sync --group licensed          # licensed machine, wheel file present
uv sync --frozen --group mock     # CI, no wheel file, no credentials

To take the licensed build from the QPerfect index instead, point its source at it as Getting Started shows.

docs.title: Under the same name
docs.text:
The two builds also share the name mimiq-tensorkeeper, so that code and imports do not change between them. In a uv project, two dependency groups that exclude each other give each environment its build from its own index:

[dependency-groups]
licensed = ["mimiq-tensorkeeper"]
mock = ["mimiq-tensorkeeper"]

[tool.uv]
# The two groups install the same package from different places, so they can
# never be installed together.
conflicts = [[{ group = "licensed" }, { group = "mock" }]]

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "qperfect"
url = "https://license.qperfect.io/pypi/simple"
explicit = true

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "pypi"
url = "https://pypi.org/simple"
explicit = true

[tool.uv.sources]
mimiq-tensorkeeper = [
  { index = "qperfect", group = "licensed" },
  { index = "pypi", group = "mock" },
]

The lockfile records both builds, so creating or updating it needs the QPerfect credentials (UV_INDEX_QPERFECT_USERNAME=mimiq and your token as UV_INDEX_QPERFECT_PASSWORD). Installing does not, for the mock:

uv sync --group licensed          # licensed machine
uv sync --frozen --group mock     # CI, no credentials needed

If you receive the licensed build as a wheel file rather than from the index, use a path for the licensed source instead: { path = "wheels/mimiq_tensorkeeper-<version>-<tags>.whl", group = "licensed" }.

The public build is published with the same version numbers as the licensed one, but may lag behind it. Check that the version CI installs is the one you test against.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: TensorKeeper runs on threads it does not create itself. The linear algebra runs on the threads of the BLAS or of faer, and sampling runs on a rayon pool. This page covers how many of each a run gets, how to change it, and how to check what a run actually used.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: You want Do One count for everything, for the whole process export MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS=8 before starting Python Different counts for evolution and sampling MIMIQ_CORE_NUM_THREADS and MIMIQ_SAMPLER_NUM_THREADS A cap for the runs of one simulator TkSimulator(max_num_threads=4) To run inside a container or a batch allocation Set MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS to the CPUs you were given (see Containers and batch jobs) To see what a run resolved tensorkeeper.thread_info()

docs.title: The two pools
docs.text:
Pool What runs on it Sized by core Linear algebra on the residual MPS: dressed gates, sums, compression. MIMIQ_CORE_NUM_THREADS sampler Drawing shots from the evolved state. MIMIQ_SAMPLER_NUM_THREADS

Both fall back to MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS when their own variable is unset, so the common case is one variable:

export MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS=8      # both pools, eight threads each

and the uncommon case is two:

export MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS=8          # eight by default
export MIMIQ_SAMPLER_NUM_THREADS=2  # except sampling, which gets two

The pools scale differently, which is why they are separate. The core pool parallelizes inside each tensor contraction, which pays off only when the residual's bond dimension is large. On Clifford-dominated circuits it often stays small, and extra core threads then cost more than they save. The sampler pool parallelizes across shots, which pays off whenever you ask for many shots.

Set the variables before the first run: the core count is applied when the engine first runs, while the sampler count is read on every sampling call.

docs.title: Capping one simulator
docs.text:
max_num_threads caps both pools for the runs of one simulator, without touching the environment:

from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator

# At most four threads for this simulator's runs, whatever the process has.
sim = TkSimulator(bonddim=128, max_num_threads=4)
results = sim.execute(circuit, nsamples=1000)

TkSimulatorGpu takes it too. The cap is a ceiling over what the variables give: a process sized to two threads stays at two under max_num_threads=4. It is held for the length of each execute and evolve call and released when the call returns.

The pools are process-wide, so two simulators running at the same time on different Python threads share them. Each then runs at the smallest cap either holds.

docs.title: What resolves to what
docs.text:
For each pool, in order, with any max_num_threads cap applied on top:

  1. that pool's own MIMIQ_* variable,
  2. MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS,
  3. the native variable of the library underneath, which that library reads for itself,
  4. nothing, and the library sizes itself.

A value that is not a positive integer is ignored and the next name in the order is consulted.

The native variables depend on the engine (linalg):

Engine Core pool reads Default with nothing set "openblas" OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS, OMP_NUM_THREADS one thread per CPU in the affinity mask "mkl" MKL_NUM_THREADS, OMP_NUM_THREADS one thread per physical core "faer" RAYON_NUM_THREADS one thread per CPU the process may use, counting a CPU quota

The sampler reads RAYON_NUM_THREADS on every engine. Prefer the MIMIQ_* names: they mean the same thing on every engine, while OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS does nothing on MKL and MKL_NUM_THREADS nothing on OpenBLAS.

docs.title: Containers and batch jobs
docs.text:
The default count comes from the CPU affinity mask, which taskset, numactl and Slurm's CPU binding all set, so a run inside such an allocation sizes itself to it.

A CPU quota is different. docker --cpus, a Kubernetes limits.cpu and a cgroup cpu.max limit CPU time but leave the affinity mask at the whole machine, so OpenBLAS and MKL still start one thread per machine CPU, and those threads fight over the quota. Under a quota, always set the count:

export MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS=2   # the CPUs the container was given

Never set a count above the CPUs the job was given. An oversubscribed BLAS does not slow down gently: runs can take many times longer.

docs.title: Checking what a run resolved
docs.text:
>>> import tensorkeeper as tk
>>> tk.thread_info()
{'core': {'source': 'MIMIQ_NUM_THREADS', 'threads': 8, 'effective': 8},
 'sampler': {'source': 'MIMIQ_SAMPLER_NUM_THREADS', 'threads': 2}}
  • source names what decided the count: a variable, "limit" while a max_num_threads cap holds it down, or "unset".
  • threads is the count requested. None means no MIMIQ_* variable applied and the library sized itself.
  • effective (core only) is the count the linear algebra actually runs on. A request the library did not take shows up as a difference between threads and effective.

tk.thread_info() reports the default engine. Each engine is a separate library with its own counts, so for a simulator on another engine pass its name: tk.thread_info(linalg="mkl").

A typo in a variable shows up here as a source you did not expect, not as an error.

Results are not bitwise identical across thread counts: a different count changes the order of floating-point sums, so fidelities and amplitudes agree to about 1e-13 relative, not to the last bit. Compare runs with a tolerance.

docs.title: Accuracy and Tuning
docs.text: What each setting does, when to change it, and how to tell whether a result is trustworthy. The short version: leave the defaults alone until a fidelity tells you not to.

docs.title: The settings
docs.text:
All configuration is construction-only. A state carries the settings it was built with, so build a new simulator to change one.

from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator

sim = TkSimulator(
    bonddim=256,             # cap on the MPS bond dimension
    sv_cutoff=1e-8,          # singular values below this are discarded
    disentangle_period=1,    # N = every N MPS operations, "auto", 0 = off
)

All three trade accuracy against time and memory. Reproducibility is not a simulator setting: pass seed= to execute (see Randomness). Nothing about bond dimension or fidelity depends on the seed: with no measurement in the circuit, the evolution is deterministic.

docs.title: bonddim
docs.text:
The maximum bond dimension the residual MPS may use. Reaching it forces truncation, which loses fidelity.

An \(n\)-qubit state cannot exceed \(\chi = 2^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}\), so for small registers the default 256 can never truncate. It starts to bind when the circuit's magic grows: bond dimension in \(|\varphi\rangle\) tracks the non-Clifford content, so what matters is the \(T\) count, not the qubit count.

Raise it when the fidelity drops below what you can accept. Cost grows roughly as \(\chi^3\), so doubling it is roughly eight times the work. Lower it to trade accuracy for speed and memory on a deliberately approximate run.

docs.title: sv_cutoff
docs.text:
During compression, singular values below this fraction of the largest one are discarded, whatever bonddim allows. The default 1e-8 is numerical hygiene rather than approximation: far below any physically meaningful weight, but large enough to prune the numerical noise that would otherwise make bonds creep upward for no benefit.

Raise it (1e-4, 1e-3) to trade a controlled amount of fidelity for a smaller bond dimension on a circuit that is too big at the cutoff you have. It is the gentler of the two truncation knobs, because it drops weight that is genuinely small instead of whatever does not fit. Leave it alone for exact work.

Do not set it to zero, or below about 1e-16. There you stop pruning noise and start retaining bonds that carry nothing, which costs time and memory and buys no accuracy.

docs.title: disentangle_period
docs.text:
Controls the Clifford disentangler: a periodic sweep that looks for two-qubit Cliffords lowering the entanglement of \(|\varphi\rangle\), applies them to the MPS and compensates them in the frame. It moves entanglement from the MPS into the frame, where it is free. The re-split is exact, so enabling it can never change the answer on a run that was not truncating.

Value Behavior 1 (default) sweep after every MPS-touching operation N sweep every N MPS-touching operations "auto" adaptive: sweep after an operation that grew the bond dimension; the period doubles whenever a sweep fails to reduce it, and resets as soon as one succeeds 0 never sweep

It is on by default because a lower bond dimension makes every later MPS operation cheaper (their cost grows as \(\chi^3\)), so the sweeps usually pay for themselves. On magic state cultivation workloads around 92% of the peak bond dimension is recoverable this way: a shot of msc_d5_noisy runs 7× faster with 1 than with 0. When a run saturates bonddim, recovering even a factor of two in the residual also converts directly into accuracy.

"auto" is eager while sweeps keep collapsing \(\chi\) and backs off once they stop, so it suits a circuit the disentangler helps only now and then. Set 0 only for a circuit that never accumulates gauge entanglement.

The disentangler affects the fidelity claim

The sweep compresses at sv_cutoff, and the MPS engine does not report how much weight a compression discarded. Once a sweep has run, the result can no longer claim exactness, even if nothing was in fact lost.

docs.title: Reading the fidelity
docs.text:
evolve returns (state, fidelity), and execute fills results.fidelities. There are two answers:

from mimiqcircuits.backends import ExactFidelity, TruncationLowerBound

ExactFidelity(): the bonddim cap never bound. Before each operation that can grow a bond, every bond had room to grow by that operation's full factor (twice for a rotation, a two-site gate or a disentangler gate, the number of terms for a wide Pauli sum), so nothing the cap would cut was ever at risk. A pure Clifford circuit always reports this, and so does a circuit with magic at a generous bonddim.

TruncationLowerBound(v): the cap bound at least once, and the fidelity is at least v, the weight that survived.

Weight dropped below sv_cutoff counts against neither: it is the tolerance you asked for. At the default 1e-8 that is numerical noise, but a raised sv_cutoff can lose real accuracy while the claim still reads ExactFidelity(). Validate a run with a raised cutoff against one at the default.

docs.title: Why TruncationLowerBound(1.0) is not ExactFidelity()
docs.text:
The two are different claims:

  • ExactFidelity() says the cap never could have cut anything.
  • TruncationLowerBound(1.0) says the cap was reached, and nothing is known to have been cut.

An operation that reached the cap and happened to discard nothing gives the second, not the first. The distinction is about what could have been lost, and weakening the claim is the honest thing to do when the cap was in play. You will meet TruncationLowerBound(1.0) when bonddim is just large enough for the state, the edge where raising it is cheap insurance.

Treat any TruncationLowerBound as a signal to check convergence, even at 1.0.

docs.title: What the number is
docs.text:
The reported value is a product of per-step retained weights: the surviving norm of the state. That is exact for a single truncation, but across many steps it is an estimate rather than a guarantee, and it can read higher than the true overlap with the untruncated state.

A truncated state is left unnormalized, which gives you a second, independent reading of the same quantity. Probabilities over all basis states sum to the weight that actually survived rather than to 1:

from mimiqcircuits import BitString

total = sum(state.probability(BitString.fromint(n, i)) for i in range(2 ** n))
print(total)      # 1.0 on an exact run; the surviving weight on a truncated one

On a mildly truncated run that sum matches the reported number. When it comes back well below the reported number, the report is optimistic and the run is badly truncated. Read a low fidelity as "do not trust this run", not as a percentage of correctness.

Give the cap headroom

Setting bonddim to exactly the bond dimension the state needs leaves no room, and the run can come back with weight missing from the probabilities while the reported bound still reads 0.99…. Leave the cap some headroom, and confirm accuracy with the convergence sweep below rather than from the reported number alone.

docs.title: Checking convergence
docs.text:
The reliable method is a bond-dimension sweep. Run the same circuit at increasing bonddim and watch the quantity you care about stop moving:

import mimiqcircuits as mc
from tensorkeeper import TkSimulator

# A deliberately magic-dense circuit: a T on every qubit in every layer, so
# truncation actually bites. This is the regime where tuning matters.
n = 12
c = mc.Circuit()
for _ in range(12):
    for q in range(n):
        c.push(mc.GateH(), q)
        c.push(mc.GateT(), q)
    for q in range(0, n - 1, 2):
        c.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)
    for q in range(1, n - 1, 2):
        c.push(mc.GateCX(), q, q + 1)

for chi in (4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128):
    sim = TkSimulator(bonddim=chi)
    state = sim.build_state(n)
    state, fidelity = sim.evolve(state, sim.compile(c))
    amp = state.amplitude(mc.BitString("0" * n))
    print(f"chi={chi:4d}  bond={state.bond_dim:4d}  amp={amp.real:.8f}  {fidelity}")

chi=   4  bond=   4  amp=0.00193885  TruncationLowerBound(value=0.0075457069804879375)
chi=   8  bond=   8  amp=0.00758821  TruncationLowerBound(value=0.03899335457021127)
chi=  16  bond=  16  amp=0.02081354  TruncationLowerBound(value=0.12923164205102064)
chi=  32  bond=  32  amp=0.02032901  TruncationLowerBound(value=0.4027227961193784)
chi=  64  bond=  64  amp=0.02394088  TruncationLowerBound(value=0.9999999999999301)
chi= 128  bond=  64  amp=0.02394088  TruncationLowerBound(value=0.9999999999999301)

Converged at \(\chi = 64\): the amplitude stopped moving, the fidelity reached 1 to numerical precision, and raising the cap to 128 left the bond dimension at 64, which means nothing was being truncated any more. The intermediate rows are the warning. At \(\chi = 16\) the amplitude looks plausible and is wrong by 13%, and the fidelity of 0.13 was telling you so.

Do not judge convergence from the fidelity alone: it bounds the truncation loss, not the error in any particular observable.

docs.title: Diagnosing cost
docs.text:
If a circuit is slower or larger than you expected, bond_dim is the first thing to look at.

print(state.bond_dim)
  • \(\chi = 1\) and it should not be. Two innocent explanations before you suspect a problem. The circuit may be genuinely all Clifford: a rotation at a Clifford angle, \(R_Z(\pi/2)\) for example, is absorbed by the frame. Or the magic is real but still free, which is normal for the first order-\(n\) non-Clifford gates on a wide register.
  • \(\chi\) larger than the \(T\) count suggests. The dressed gates are landing on wide supports. If you turned the disentangler off or slowed it down, set disentangle_period=1 back.
  • \(\chi\) pinned at bonddim. You are truncating. Raise the cap, and expect a TruncationLowerBound.
  • \(\chi\) at the \(2^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}\) ceiling. The residual has become a generic state and the frame is buying you nothing. This is the magic-everywhere regime where TensorKeeper is the wrong tool; see When to use it.

Remember that this number describes \(|\varphi\rangle\), not \(|\psi\rangle\). See Concepts.
